newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Riot-hit Indonesian towns quiet but tense.
newsitem.headline: Riot-hit Indonesian towns quiet but tense.

text.p: Calm returned on Friday to riot-hit towns on Indonesia's main Java island, but troops guarded areas where violence erupted this week.
Residents in Wonosobo, the scene of fighting between supporters of the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the ruling Golkar party on Wednesday, said the town was peaceful but tense.
At least three government offices, 11 vehicles and dozens of homes were damaged and 14 people were injured in Wonosobo in clashes between PPP and Golkar supporters, newspapers have said.
On Friday, there was little evidence of the violence and police refused comment. Wonosobo is in Central Java province and 350 km (215 miles) southeast of Jakarta.
But one resident said a PPP function was held in the town on Wednesday and there were rumours beforehand that violence could ensue.

"As a result, about 120 riot police were at the function and it passed off peacefully," said the resident, who said his name was Dadit. But fighting broke out when people who attended the gathering were on their way home.

One group, from the neighbouring town of Banjarnegara, clashed with Golkar supporters just outside Wonosobo, residents said. The site, on the main road to Banjarnegara, was being guarded by troops and riot police on Friday.
Tension between PPP and Golkar cadres has been high since riots two weeks ago in the coastal town of Pekalongan, also in Central Java and a PPP stronghold.
The fighting erupted after a popular folk singer, who has campaigned for the PPP in the past, announced he would be a candidate in the May 29 general elections.
A senior official of the Indonesian military said Central Java was prone to violence.
The official Antara news agency quoted Major-General Soebagyo, the military commander for Central Java, as saying the area's demographic characteristics made it prone to violence.
The comments were believed to be a reference to the high population density in the region and the sharply-defined political loyalties among its people.
On the streets of the towns in the area and on the highways winding through rice paddies, there was much evidence of the coming election, although the official campaign does not begin until April 27.

Flags in the yellow colour of Golkar and the green of the PPP were flying. The trunks of trees along the highway were painted yellow and a man hanging up an advertisement banner for a retail chain said government officials had insisted that the background be yellow.
Only three political parties -- the PPP, Golkar and the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) -- are allowed to contest the elections.
In the last parliamentary elections in 1992, Golkar won 68 percent of the vote, the PPP 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent.
Golkar is certain to win this year's polls, but party leaders have said they want to increase their vote to above 70 percent.
